transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-28 14:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Lena Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (SE), Aisha Patel (Redwood SE), Ravi Menon (CTO, PolarWave), Claire Zhao (ML Platform), Marcus Lee (SRE), Sana Iqbal (Product)

[00:00] Lena Kim: Okay everyone, welcome. Uh, quick roll call, and then we'll jump into the numbers that Diego prepared.
[00:12] Ravi Menon: Yep, here. Thanks for doing this. We had some spikes overnight so curious what you saw.
[00:18] Diego Morales: Morning — afternoon — yeah. I pulled the trial logs, I ran the same 6-hour window that's been our baseline and also a 1-hour high-load window where you see the long tail.
[00:29] Claire Zhao: Just to flag, we pushed a minor routing tweak this morning so some of the traffic went to the cheaper replica.
[00:34] Diego Morales: noted, okay. So top-level: baseline tokens per second per GPU at your current profile is about 75k tokens/sec per V100-equivalent per hour? sorry per minute — um, per GPU sustained at median. That maps to roughly 2.1M tokens per GPU per hour. Cost math we ran: at hosted rates in the pilot (your pilot discount applied) that's about 0.45 tokens per dollar? no, 0.45 dollars per thousand tokens — mm I need to be careful — essentially the unit econ is $0.0045 per 1k tokens on the high-quality model. When we enable prefix caching for your common 300–800 token prompts, effective tokens generated drops ~18–26% depending on hit rate.
[01:20] Marcus Lee: Wait can you repeat the cache savings? 18 to 26 percent on token generation?
[01:24] Diego Morales: yeah, so that's tokens avoided on the model side because the KV cache returns the prefix. So end-to-end tokens billed to you are lower, and latency improves for cached ones. Our run showed 22% average savings for your sample.
[01:33] Sana Iqbal: How much does caching change tail latency? We've seen a few requests take 2.3 seconds which kills UX.
[01:38] Diego Morales: Good call — cached responses were in the 200–300ms range median, uncached median was ~690ms, tail 95th was about 2.1s in the no-cache scenario. With caching on and high hit rate, tail falls below 800ms. But if your batch window grows we started to see the 95th creep back up.
[01:53] Ravi Menon: Hmm, batching tradeoffs — we want throughput but not latency for interactive flows. Do you recommend micro-batching?
[01:59] Aisha Patel: For interactive product surfaces micro-batching (20–40ms window) gives you modest throughput gains with negligible user-perceived latency. For async background tasks you can bump to larger windows and much better tokens/sec per dollar.
[02:12] Marcus Lee: Can you quantify the tokens/sec per dollar delta for those batch windows?
[02:16] Diego Morales: Roughly: 20ms window -> 10–12% improved throughput vs no batching. 50ms -> 27–32%. 200ms -> around 65% improvement but 95th latency goes up substantially. For your request distribution, moving from 20ms to 50ms gives the best sweet spot for mixed interactive + batch, about 18% better tokens/sec per dollar while keeping 95th under 1s with caching enabled.
[02:40] Claire Zhao: What about quantization? We tried an 8-bit run and saw quality dip on a few legal prompts.
[02:46] Diego Morales: Right, that's the classic tradeoff. We ran 8-bit symmetric quant on the model and the perplexity jump was small on general prompts but visible on corner cases — legal text and some code fragments. 4-bit (int4) gains are larger (~2.2x tokens/sec per dollar on serving cost) but quality regressions are bigger. We recommended a hybrid: route safety/legal/regulatory prompts to the full-precision variant and background analytics to int4 or 8-bit. Redwood's routing policy can do that per route.
[03:13] Ravi Menon: Are those routing rules something you can ship in the pilot config or do we need to instrument at our side?
[03:18] Lena Kim: We can propose a pilot config and a traffic-splitting policy. Diego can build an example ruleset that matches text length and flagged categories, and Claire can tweak it.
[03:25] Diego Morales: Yep, I'll draft the ruleset. Also note: cache keying matters. We saw a bunch of cache misses because the app appends user timestamps to the prefix; normalizing keys increased hit rate by 14%.
[03:36] Claire Zhao: Ah yes, we do append small session tokens client-side — we can strip those server-side. Good catch.
[03:40] Sana Iqbal: On the billing side, there was a surprise where mid-month we spiked cost by 18% — can the token-econ workbook show which routes caused it?
[03:47] Lena Kim: We'll break it down. Diego, can you include per-route tokens per dollar and hit-rate contribution?
[03:52] Diego Morales: Yep, I'll export a per-route CSV and a pivot for the top 10 routes. Expect that in the workbook.
[03:57] Marcus Lee: On the infra side, we're worried about KV cache memory pressure. If we increase TTLs to improve hit rate, will memory blow out?
[04:03] Diego Morales: Good question. We did simulation with your 1.2M unique prefix keys over a 24h window. If you increase TTL from 10 minutes to 60 minutes, memory footprint goes up ~4x but hit rate improves another 9–11%. There's a middle ground: a two-tier TTL where hot prefixes get longer TTLs and cold prefixes are evicted faster. Redwood supports weighted TTLs via the console rules.
[04:25] Ravi Menon: Two-tier TTL sounds promising. Claire, can your team annotate hot prefixes?
[04:29] Claire Zhao: Yeah, we can surface the top 5% by frequency and we can also send a small list to Redwood.
[04:34] Diego Morales: Perfect. Also on routing, for low-priority analytic jobs we suggested routing to a cheaper model variant, roughly 40% lower cost per token. Diego: that's the small model with a 1.2x latency improvement?
[04:45] Aisha Patel: it's actually a tiny-1 variant — cost is lower but you lose some long-form coherence. fine for summarization or classification where human review exists.
[04:52] Sana Iqbal: Okay, so tactical ask: run the 24h bench with (A) current profile, (B) +prefix key normalization + TTL tweaks, (C) +micro-batching 50ms, (D) +quantization hybrid routing. Show tokens/sec/dollar and 95th latency for each.
05:03] Diego Morales: noted, we'll run those four scenarios. Any preference for the trace to use — your production-like 24h or synth?
[05:09] Marcus Lee: Prod-like is better. I'll put the anonymized trace in the shared S3 and give you access.
[05:13] Lena Kim: We'll attach the workbook and a short README describing the bench. Diego will lead the run.
[05:18] Ravi Menon: One more question — for the evaluation, do you include cache operational cost? From our side, there's memory and small extra egress for cache misses.
[05:25] Diego Morales: Yes, we include the cache storage amortized cost and the extra CPU for key normalization. Overall net econ still positive for your profile, but margin changes slightly depending on TTL. We'll include a column for cache amortized cost.
[05:36] Sana Iqbal: Security/compliance note — will the bench contain PII? We have to scrub before upload.
[05:40] Claire Zhao: We'll anonymize the trace. Marcus will scrub.
[05:43] Marcus Lee: Yep, I'll run the sanitization job.
[05:46] Lena Kim: Cool — recap: Diego runs 24h bench across four scenarios, Lena shares workbook today, Marcus uploads trace by April 1, Claire confirms cache key normalization and hot-list, and we'll schedule the SE test next week. Any final?
[05:58] Ravi Menon: Sounds good, thanks. Appreciate the concrete numbers.
[06:02] Lena Kim: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in the thread with the spreadsheet.
[06:06] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., model variant names) — speakers sometimes overlap.
